lines.text: Your buttons are bound, but none of that code has turned a motor yet. Now the laptop plays the robot controller, and everything past it is real.
Tuner X and your program can't both have the devices. Turn that switch back off, or no motor ever answers your code.
These are real motors. Clear the arm's path, and know where Disable is.
Two entries sit right next to each other in this menu. Pick the one with Hardware in its name. The other fakes the motors, and your bench won't move.
Drag your controller onto the first slot. That's the port your code listens on.
Pick Teleoperated, then your OpMode under it. Your real devices show up on the right, and an empty list means you started the wrong simulator.
Enable, and nothing moves, which is correct. Every command is waiting on a button. Hold one and the mechanism runs, then let go and the release binding takes over.
So what about a binding with no release? This diagram follows one press from the controller, through your code, out to the motor controller.
Hold the button, and the command sends six volts every loop while the motor runs. Now let go.
The command is gone and the motor's still turning. Canceling a command sends the motor nothing, so it carries on with its last request.
Tick the box, and the release gets a command of its own, one that sends the motor something new.
Try it again. Hold the button, let go, and watch what reaches the motor this time.
A request stays on the motor until another one replaces it. For every button you bind, decide what the release sends.
A real robot gets this same program from the same menu. Next the arm gets a target instead of a voltage, and there a request that stays put is exactly what you want.
